notes.meaning: The queen of Sheba most likely ruled in southern Arabia, south of Israel. She heard how famous Solomon was, a fame that came from the LORD and the great things God had done for him. She came to test his wisdom with hard questions, like riddles. Matthew Henry adds that she wanted to learn, most of all about Solomon's God. Jesus later points to her in Matthew 12:42 to shame people who will not come to hear Him, who is greater than Solomon.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars say the place of Sheba is still unsettled. Since old lists of Sheba's rulers name only kings, they think a queen is historically unlikely. They see the story's purpose as showing that Solomon's wisdom was famous even at the edge of the known world.

notes.meaning: She came in style, with a long line of camels, as royal travellers did in Arabia. Her camels carried spices, gold and jewels, which were the riches of her own land. She did not come to beg. She brought plenty. Then she told Solomon everything she had in mind to ask.

Solomon answered every question, and nothing was too hard for him. Riddles and puzzles were a big part of how people in the East tested wisdom. Matthew Henry says Solomon made things easy that she thought could not be solved. He believes Solomon surely taught her about God and His worship too.

The queen saw Solomon's wisdom and his palace. She also saw his rich table, the well-ordered places of his officials, the servants in fine clothes, and his cupbearers. She saw the many burnt offerings he gave at the temple. Some older translations say she saw the special stairway he used to go up to the temple instead. It was all so amazing that she was left breathless, almost faint.

She admits the reports she heard back home were true. She had not believed them until she saw for herself. In fact, the truth was more than twice as great as the stories. Matthew Henry says people who come to know God find the same thing: not half was told them. In heaven, even less of the joy will have been told (1 Corinthians 2:9).

She calls Solomon's servants blessed, because they get to hear his wisdom every day. Matthew Henry notes that many people have such a privilege and don't value it. The Geneva Notes add that those who hear God's wisdom in His Word are even happier. The same is true of those who serve Christ.

She praises the LORD for delighting in Solomon and putting him on Israel's throne. This was God's own choice and a sign of His lasting love for Israel. She reminds Solomon that God made him king to do what is fair and right, not to live in luxury. Commentators differ on whether she truly came to faith. Some think it possible, while others think it was polite respect for Israel's God.

She gave Solomon a huge gift of gold, more spices than ever came again, and precious stones. Matthew Henry links this to Psalm 72:15, which speaks of the gold of Sheba being given to the king. He also links it to the wise men's gifts to Jesus. Christ does not need our gifts, but He welcomes them as our thanks.

These verses are a side note. Talk of her gifts reminds the writer of what Hiram's ships brought from Ophir: gold, jewels and rare almug wood. That wood may have been sandalwood or a fragrant fir. Solomon used it for steps or railings in the temple and palace, and for harps and lyres for the singers. Such fine wood was never seen again.

Solomon gave her all she asked for. He also gave her generous gifts, as was the custom between kings. Then she went home with her servants. Matthew Henry says those who come to Jesus find Him even kinder. He does more for us than we can ask or think.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An Ethiopian tradition says she had a son by Solomon, named Menelik. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls this tradition fairly recent and not supported by early sources.

notes.meaning: Each year Solomon took in 666 talents of gold, a huge amount, probably given as a round number. On top of that came taxes from traders, tribute from Arabian kings, and payments from local governors. His support of trade and his forts along the trade routes made him rich. Matthew Henry notes that 666 is a gloomy number (see Revelation 13:18).

differ.view: Some evangelicals see a link between this 666 and the number of the beast. They suggest the Antichrist may be like Solomon, a gifted man spoiled by power and wealth.

notes.meaning: Solomon made 500 shields covered with hammered gold, in two sizes. They were kept in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a hall of his palace. His guards carried them on special occasions. Gold is too soft for battle, so they were for show. Matthew Henry sees shields as a sign that a good ruler protects good people.

Solomon's throne was decorated with ivory and covered with fine gold. It had six steps, a rounded back, and armrests with a lion beside each one. Twelve more lions stood on the steps. Lions were a sign of royal power, and the twelve may stand for Israel's twelve tribes. Matthew Henry says the lions reminded the king to judge boldly. No other kingdom had a throne like it.

Even Solomon's cups and dishes were gold, so silver hardly counted. Matthew Henry draws a lesson: plenty of anything makes it seem cheap. If gold made silver seem worthless, then God's grace and the hope of heaven should make gold seem small to us.

Solomon's ships sailed with Hiram's fleet and came back every three years. They brought gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks. No one is sure where Tarshish was. Matthew Henry worries that apes and peacocks show a people growing childish from too much wealth.

Solomon became greater than any king on earth in riches and wisdom. People from everywhere came to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. Each year they brought gifts as tribute: silver, gold, clothes, weapons, spices, horses and mules. Matthew Henry reminds us that Christ is greater than Solomon.

Solomon built up a large force of chariots and horses. He kept them in special chariot cities and in Jerusalem. Many commentators see a warning here. God had told Israel's kings not to pile up horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), so that they would trust Him for protection. Others note that a strong defence may have helped keep the peace.

This is a vivid way of saying that silver and fine cedar became as common as stones and ordinary fig trees. Matthew Henry says Solomon did not hoard his riches. The whole kingdom shared in them. He sees this as a picture of Christ, who makes His people rich.

Solomon's traders bought horses and chariots from Egypt and Kue, perhaps a place near Egypt's border. They also sold them on to the Hittite and Aramean kings. Matthew Henry notes that a great king did not think trade was beneath him. Adam Clarke points out that God had forbidden kings to bring in horses from Egypt, and Solomon ignored this.
